label: Treat your metrics as a product with named customers
rationale: Converts a permanent political argument about engineering productivity into an ordinary product problem: identify three customer groups (engineers, engineering managers, leaders outside engineering), do user research, ship a small first version, improve it over time. This is the essay's selected payoff.

label: What decision would you make differently if you knew this?
rationale: One portable question that kills unfounded metric requests and reframes them toward the real underlying question ("Are we okay?"). The most reusable single move in the book; observed working in the running case study against a GitHub-contribution-graph MVP claim.

label: Every answer gets a metric, a success criterion, and a maintenance goal
rationale: Table 10-1 decomposes a high-level business question into a specific question, explicit success criteria (CI under 15 min, CI/CD under 30 min), named metrics, and a maintenance goal (95% of runs). Turns vague measurement talk into a fillable spec.

label: DORA four plus one or two context metrics, five or six total
rationale: Caps the working set, ties the extra metrics to the current worst pain (reliability / predictability / quality / team health), and prescribes a rollout: baseline four to six weeks, then add context, then reassess quarterly which metrics drove a decision.

label: Inventory what you already emit before buying a platform
rationale: Git, CI/CD, issue tracking, and monitoring usually already contain all four DORA metrics. Author-reported: more than one team was about to buy an expensive metrics platform and found the data in Jira, GitHub, and CircleCI.

label: Measure teams, not individuals; context not judgment
rationale: The safety requirement that stops the product framing becoming a surveillance system. Includes a concrete failure: publishing per-reviewer PR review time caused rubber-stamping and tripled bug escape rate in two weeks.

label: Goodhart's Law, context ignorance, and invisible work
rationale: Three named ways a measurement product degrades. The invisible-work argument is the strongest: the fix is not measuring more but stating what you are NOT measuring, rotating focus metrics, and protecting time for unmeasured work.

label: Version metrics like code; give them an owner; retire them
rationale: Minor/major version bumps, a changelog when a calculation changes, a named owner acting as product manager for the metrics, and an explicit deletion check. Unusually concrete for a leadership book and what makes "product" more than a metaphor.

label: Velocity is a capacity planning tool, not a productivity metric
rationale: Keep it inside the team, read it as a rolling average, treat sharp moves as a signal to investigate. Useful but narrower than the rest; optional in the reading mission unless story points are a live argument.

label: The layered stack: people/safety, direction, process, metrics as compass
rationale: Chapter 11's synthesis. Explains why the metrics chapter is second-to-last rather than first, and supplies the essay's closing frame. Recapitulates rather than adds, so it supports the payoff instead of being it.

label: Pick one thing, commit for a month, then add one more
rationale: Chapter 11's implementation advice, structurally identical to the metrics rollout. Genuine but generic; used as corroboration only.

label: AI changes the measurements, not the methodology
rationale: Segment AI-assisted from traditional work, watch quality alongside speed, add a trust dimension. Currency-relevant for a 2026 edition, but the specific productivity figures are 2025-era snapshots.
